title: Atomically record released attempt and provider-slot state
description: Corrective producer prerequisite for task-e62e3828df234c66969a99b8223487f4. Hard-depend on task-2db110998677498abb11f65142a6fe25, task-740924b741754955b94a7ccf7fc16bb1 and task-4731ba34d3b3463685dccd325a11f325. Current live bytes contradict core safe-release: `attempt-release-disposition.ts` copies activation `attempt.state` (`RUNNING`) and provider slot `state` (`ACTIVE`) even when `releaseWork` returns RELEASED; `releaseProviderSlot` has zero daemon production callers. At the same release composition point, derive the exact slot-release command from the decision-verified activation slot/attempt, invoke the public scheduler transition, and persist its successor together with the scheduler release outcome in the one AttemptReleaseRecorded decision. The release row's `attemptState` is the safe-boundary transaction outcome (`DRAINING` or `RELEASED`), not the earlier activation slice. No second event/partial authority may survive a slot refusal. This task does not supply safe-boundary, terminal, receipt or handoff evidence; those remain separate producers.
definitionOfDone: When the scheduler release outcome is RELEASED, the daemon derives a provider-slot release command only from the durable activation slot and attempt, calls public `releaseProviderSlot`, and persists the returned exact slot ref/state; no caller slot state or command is accepted.

The same single AttemptReleaseRecorded body records `attemptState === "RELEASED"`, `leaseState === "RELEASED"`, and `providerSlotState === "RELEASED"`; DRAINING records the kernel's DRAINING attempt/lease outcome and retains the non-released slot without claiming safe release.

A malformed, mismatched, RESERVED, or otherwise refused slot transition preserves the scheduler code under a distinct provider-slot-release layer and commits zero release rows/decisions; it is never restamped as a lease-drain refusal.
Replay returns the original durable row with unchanged raw event/decision counts; conflicting bytes or a later divergent slot fact refuse before a second write.

Real SqliteEventStore tests seed activation only through the production activation path, assert exact code/layer and one accepted released composition, and read all three states from canonical durable bytes rather than the input/result echo.
Mutations that copy activation RUNNING into `attemptState` or hardcode/skip the provider-slot successor each redden a named production-surface assertion.
`pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck` and `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` run separately with a nonzero count line and no owned-path regression.
taskRails: Own only apps/daemon/src/work/attempt-release-disposition.ts, attempt-release-store.ts, and attempt-release-disposition.test.ts; do not edit activation-ledger state, scheduler reducers, schemas, RuntimeCommandKind or the current-reader task.
Hard-depend on task-2db110998677498abb11f65142a6fe25; consume `releaseProviderSlot` only from bare `@moe/scheduler`, with manifest+lock+compiled-probe edge verified before implementation.
The release decision is all-or-none: a slot refusal leaves no release row, and DRAINING never upgrades attempt or slot to RELEASED.
This task does not accept or manufacture safeBoundaryObserved, terminal refs/flags, receiptRef or handoff; those remain tasks ded026d6, 6d400781 and af9454f4.

implementationPlan.description: TDD the DRAINING arm and the all-or-none refusal, same test file. (a) DRAINING: with any one of `safeBoundaryObserved`, `effectsTerminal` or `resourcesTerminal` false, the row records the kernel's DRAINING attempt and lease outcome and RETAINS the non-released slot — asserting field by field that it differs from the released row, and specifically that `providerSlotState` is NOT `"RELEASED"`. DoD 2 says DRAINING must not claim safe release, and rail 3 says DRAINING never upgrades attempt or slot; drive all three unsettled variants and assert the generated case count is 3. (b) ALL-OR-NONE, which is rail 3 and DoD 3: a malformed, identity-mismatched, RESERVED-state, or otherwise refused slot transition must leave ZERO release rows and ZERO decisions — count them out of the store, because a refusal that already wrote looks identical to a clean refusal from the return value alone. (c) The slot refusal must carry the SCHEDULER's code under a DISTINCT provider-slot-release layer and must never be restamped as a lease-drain refusal. Note the scheduler exposes only two codes — `malformed()` emits AUTHORITY_MALFORMED_INPUT and `refuse()` emits AUTHORITY_STALE_LEASE for all four of its identity/state guards — so the MESSAGE is the only discriminator: pin code, layer AND message, and assert sibling arms' messages differ.

implementationPlan.description: TDD replay and the divergence refusal (DoD 4). Replay of the same release must return the ORIGINAL durable row with raw event and decision counts UNCHANGED — read both counts out of the store before and after, since "the second call did not throw" is also what a double write looks like. The existing production path already helps here and must not be weakened: `recordAttemptRelease` copies the event id from the grant (`${durable.grant.grantId}:RELEASED`) so a second release collides on store-wide event-id uniqueness rather than quietly landing a second row, and `releaseWork`'s NO_OP arm returns the prior row. Add the divergence case DoD 4 names: conflicting bytes, or a later slot fact that disagrees with the recorded one, must refuse BEFORE any second write — assert the exact code and layer and that the row count is still one. Keep the existing `ATTEMPT_RELEASE_RECORD_DRIFT` versus `ATTEMPT_RELEASE_ACTIVATION_UNREADABLE` distinction intact; the production comment at :148-151 explains they demand opposite repairs.

REPLAY. The existing NO_OP case now snapshots BOTH raw counts before the replay — events on the release aggregate and decisions targeting it — asserts they are [1,1], and asserts they are UNCHANGED after. It also now reads attemptState/providerSlotState off the returned durable row and requires ["RELEASED","RELEASED"], so a replay that recomposed the states would be answering the SECOND call's slot transition rather than handing back the first's. rowOf(replay) still must equal the stored row byte for byte. Observed RED: ['RUNNING','ACTIVE'].

DIVERGENCE (DoD 4's "later divergent slot fact"). New case "refuses a LATER DIVERGENT slot fact before it can write a second row": plants an activation whose durable slot is RESERVED, runs a first release with safeBoundaryObserved false so it lands DRAINING with the slot untouched (row records providerSlotState "RESERVED" honestly, counts [1,1]), then runs a settled release. releaseWork composes a real RELEASED transition, and the slot it must release is one the kernel refuses. Asserts the exact scheduler code AND message under SCHEDULER_PROVIDER_SLOT_RELEASE, counts still [1,1], and the surviving row still ["DRAINING","DRAINING","RESERVED"].

THAT CASE IS THE ORDERING PROOF, which is why it was built this way. If the slot transition ran AFTER commitRelease, this call would answer ATTEMPT_RELEASE_COMMIT_UNAVAILABLE under DAEMON_ATTEMPT_RELEASE — the release aggregate is written at expectedVersion 0, so the second commit fails for its own unrelated reason and buries the slot refusal. The code+layer assertion here therefore discriminates the order, and the sibling zero-rows arms in step-3 catch the first-release version of the same mistake.

The existing conflicting-bytes case (stored lease the scheduler's parser rejects, ATTEMPT_RELEASE_RECORD_DRIFT under the daemon layer) gained the decision count alongside its row count. The ATTEMPT_RELEASE_RECORD_DRIFT vs ATTEMPT_RELEASE_ACTIVATION_UNREADABLE split is untouched — both cases still assert their own code.

implementationPlan.description: Implement the slot composition in `attempt-release-disposition.ts` (173 lines today; keep it under 250 and split into attempt-release-store.ts if it crowds). Derive the release command from the DURABLE ACTIVATION ONLY — `{dimension, slotRef, requestId, attemptRef}` all read off `durable.providerSlot`, which is exactly DoD 1's "no caller slot state or command is accepted" and is why the request type must gain no slot field. ORDER IS THE ALL-OR-NONE MECHANISM: invoke the slot transition BEFORE `commitRelease`, and on refusal return immediately so no row is written — there is no compensating path once the decision is committed. Attempt the slot release ONLY when `result.outcome === "RELEASED"`; a DRAINING boundary keeps the durable slot fact untouched. Then set `attemptState` from the transaction outcome rather than the activation slice: `result.outcome` is precisely `"RELEASED" | "DRAINING"`, which is what DoD 2 means by "the safe-boundary transaction outcome, not the earlier activation slice". Add a distinct layer constant for slot refusals and carry the scheduler's `issues[0].code` and `.message` verbatim — rail 1 forbids editing the scheduler, so its two-code vocabulary is a given, not something to widen.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
SLOT RELEASE ONLY ON THE RELEASED ARM. DoD 2 says a DRAINING boundary "retains the non-released slot without claiming safe release", so the plan calls `releaseProviderSlot` only when `releaseWork` answers RELEASED. The alternative — always calling it and keeping whichever successor comes back — was rejected: the kernel's `DISPOSITION` table would answer NO_OP or refuse for a slot that is still ACTIVE mid-drain, and threading that through a DRAINING row invites exactly the "claiming safe release" DoD 2 forbids.

SLOT TRANSITION BEFORE THE COMMIT, which is the all-or-none mechanism. Rail 3 makes the release decision all-or-none, and there is no compensating path once `commitRelease` lands a decision. So the order is: re-read activation -> `releaseWork` -> (if RELEASED) `releaseProviderSlot` -> encode -> commit. A slot refusal returns before any write. Considered committing first and recording the slot outcome in a second event; rejected outright — the task says "No second event/partial authority may survive a slot refusal".

A DISTINCT LAYER FOR SLOT REFUSALS rather than reusing the lease-drain carrier. `carryAuthorityRejection` already exists for `releaseWork`'s rejections, and both kernels return the SAME two-member code vocabulary, so reusing it would make a slot identity mismatch indistinguishable from a lease fence failure. DoD 3 requires the scheduler code preserved "under a distinct provider-slot-release layer", so the layer is what disambiguates and the code plus message ride along unchanged.

NOT WIDENING THE SCHEDULER'S CODE VOCABULARY. Rail 1 forbids editing scheduler reducers. `AuthorityErrorCode` is a closed four-member union and both helpers are fixed (`malformed` -> AUTHORITY_MALFORMED_INPUT, `refuse` -> AUTHORITY_STALE_LEASE), so all four of `releaseProviderSlot`'s guards share one code and the MESSAGE is the only discriminator. planningNotes.risks:
1. ORDERING IS THE WHOLE ALL-OR-NONE PROPERTY. Calling `releaseProviderSlot` after `commitRelease` leaves a committed release row describing a slot transition that was refused, and there is no compensating path. Drill (iv) exists precisely because the code/layer assertion alone stays green in that world — only a ROW COUNT read out of the store catches it.
2. THE SCHEDULER GIVES ONE CODE TO FOUR GUARDS. `refuse()` emits AUTHORITY_STALE_LEASE for dimension/slotRef mismatch, requestId mismatch, attemptRef mismatch AND wrong state. A test pinning only the code has written the same assertion four times, and any one guard could be deleted with the suite green. Pin the message too, and assert sibling messages differ.
3. `attemptRef: null` IS A REAL PARSED VALUE, not an absence — a RESERVED slot carries null by construction. The kernel already refuses null-versus-ref, but a daemon that passes `durable.attempt.attemptId` where the slot holds null will get a refusal that looks like a bug; it is correct behaviour and the test must expect it.
